opus-5.5.text:
I think the key difference is in what kind of tasks you're facing and who defines them.

With o1 and o3, the core capability is reasoning on problems like math, coding, and science. Those domains have a nice property: the problem distribution is relatively well-defined, and you can verify answers. You can build a large training set, run RL on it, and the model gets very strong in that domain. Even if it doesn't generalize perfectly to everything else, you already have a useful product, because people really do want help with math and code. So you can go deep first and broaden later.

An agent like Operator is in a very different situation. Once you hand it a browser and say "go do things for the user," the task space is essentially open. Every user brings a different website, a different workflow, a different intent. One person wants to book a restaurant, another wants to fill out a government form, another wants to compare prices across five shopping sites. The web pages themselves keep changing, layouts change, pop-ups appear, logins break. You can't enumerate all of that in training. If the model only works on the hundred websites you trained on, the product basically doesn't exist from the user's point of view, because the first thing they try will probably be outside your distribution.

So for agents, generalization isn't a nice-to-have you add in version three. It's the minimum requirement for the product to be usable at all. That's why I'd say Operator needs generalization from day one, while reasoning models could get away with being specialists first.

This also changes how you do RL. For reasoning models, the hard part is mostly reward design and scaling the compute. For agents, the hard part becomes environment and task diversity. You need many different environments, many different kinds of tasks, and some way to make the model learn general strategies, like exploring a page, recovering from mistakes, asking for clarification when the instruction is ambiguous, rather than memorizing specific click sequences. In a sense, the agent problem pushes you to think much more about the "general" in general intelligence, because the real world doesn't give you a fixed benchmark.

And honestly, I think that's also why agents feel harder and slower to mature than reasoning models. The bar for "it works" is set by the long tail of real user needs, not by a test set you designed yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator faces an open-ended variety of websites, workflows, and user intents, making generalization the minimum requirement for a usable product from day one.

r002.rationale: It describes o1 and o3 as starting with well-defined domains such as math, coding, and science, so they can specialize first and broaden later.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key difference is where the model lives. o1 and o3 operate inside a closed, well-defined world. You give it a math problem or a coding task, the input is text, the output is text, and the environment doesn't fight back. You can scale up reinforcement learning on verifiable problems, and the model gets very good at reasoning within that box. Generalization is nice to have, but you can get a lot of value even if the model is only strong on the distribution you trained it on.

Operator is completely different. From day one it's thrown into the open world, the actual internet. Every website has a different layout, different buttons, different popups, and websites change every week. You can't enumerate all of them. You can't build a training set that covers every form on every booking site. So the moment a user asks it to do something on a site it has never seen, it has to transfer. If it can't, the product simply doesn't work. It's not a matter of being a bit less accurate, it's a matter of getting stuck on step two.

There's a second reason, which is about feedback. For o1-style reasoning, you have a clear reward signal. The answer is right or wrong, the code passes the tests or it doesn't. For an agent clicking around a browser, the reward is sparse and delayed, and the actions have real consequences. You can't just let it try a million random things on a real booking site. So you can't rely purely on brute-force RL inside the target environment to patch up every weakness. The model has to come in with a prior that already understands how interfaces work, what a login flow looks like, what a cart is, and then adapt with very few trials.

That's essentially the embodied intelligence problem, just in a browser instead of a robot. In robotics we learned this lesson painfully: a policy trained in one kitchen fails in the next kitchen. The internet is a million kitchens. So I'd say for Operator, generalization isn't a feature you add later. It's the precondition for the thing to exist at all.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator faces diverse, changing websites that cannot all be covered in training, so it must transfer to unseen sites from the start for the product to work.

r002.rationale: It describes o1 and o3 as working in a bounded math-and-coding setting where generalization is less essential, but does not say that their narrow initial scope lets them develop generalization gradually.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is that Operator has to act in an environment, and that environment is constantly changing. With something like o1 or o3, you can initially focus on a relatively well-defined domain, like math or coding, and demonstrate useful reasoning ability there. Operator has to deal with whatever interface it encounters.

Suppose you ask it to book a hotel. Every website has a different layout, different buttons, and a different checkout flow. Even the same website might show a pop-up or change its design. The agent has to understand that these different interfaces represent the same underlying task, and figure out what to do when something unexpected happens.

So generalization isn’t just a capability you add later to make Operator better. It’s part of what makes it useful in the first place. If it only works on the exact pages and interaction sequences it saw during training, it’s essentially a brittle automation script. Of course, o1 and o3 also need generalization, but for an agent interacting with the web, that requirement becomes immediate and very visible.

r001.rationale: The response explains that Operator encounters changing websites, layouts, and checkout flows, so it must generalize across interfaces from the outset to be useful.

r002.rationale: It says o1 and o3 can start in well-defined domains such as math or coding, but does not say that this narrower scope lets them develop generalization gradually.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key difference is that Operator has to act in an open-ended environment from the moment people start using it. With o1 and o3, you can initially focus on a relatively well-defined set of problems, like math or coding, where it’s easier to evaluate whether an answer is correct. Operator immediately encounters different websites, different interfaces, and different user workflows.

Even something that sounds simple, like booking a restaurant, can involve a website it has never seen, a pop-up appearing unexpectedly, or a button moving to a different place. You can’t train it on every possible combination. It has to understand the goal, apply what it learned in a new setting, and recover when the environment behaves differently than expected.

And because these tasks involve many steps, small mistakes compound. Being reliable on each individual action isn’t enough if it still fails halfway through the workflow. So generalization is a requirement for Operator to be useful from day one.

r001.rationale: It says Operator immediately faces different websites, interfaces, and workflows, and concludes that generalization is required from day one.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Operator with a relatively well-defined set of math or coding problems for o1 and o3, but does not say their generalization can develop gradually.
